title: Vayera: Isaac is born (Genesis 21:1–7)
hookLine: God remembers Sarah, and she says all who hear will laugh with her

cards: There are two kinds of laughter. One is the short, dry laugh when someone tells you something impossible. Oh, sure.
Right. That'll never happen. The other bursts out of you when the impossible thing happens anyway.
The baby is born. The test comes back clear. The person you gave up on walks through the door.
Almost the same sound, from a completely different place. Sarah laughs both ways in this portion. Today, the second laugh.

teach.b: A few chapters back, three visitors came to Abraham's tent, and one said: this time next year, Sarah will have a son. Sarah, about ninety, was listening from inside the tent.
She laughed to herself: after I'm worn out, and my husband is old, shall I have pleasure? God asked Abraham: why did Sarah laugh?

teach.h: IS ANY THING TOO HARD FOR THE LORD?
teach.b: "Is any thing too hard for the LORD?" Sarah, afraid, said, I didn't laugh. The answer came back: no, you did laugh.
That was the first laugh. Now, chapter twenty-one. God remembered Sarah, as promised, and did for her as God had spoken.
In her old age, at exactly the time foretold, she gives birth to a son.
Abraham names him Yitzchak, Isaac, which means he will laugh. And Sarah says: God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh with me.
Then, almost in wonder: who would have told Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? The same laugh, turned inside out, from disbelief to joy. And she doesn't keep it to herself.

Rashi, following the midrash, says that when Sarah was remembered, many other childless women were remembered with her, many sick people were healed, many prayers were answered, and there was laughter in the whole world.
This chapter is read in synagogues on the first day of Rosh Hashanah; the tradition says Sarah was remembered on that day.
So every Jewish year begins with a laugh that turned from doubt to joy.

how: Genesis 21 is read in synagogues on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, when, tradition says, Sarah was remembered; the birth of Isaac is often taught alongside Sarah's two laughs.

o: and she laughed, Sarah's word in the tent
and he appeared, the portion's opening word
and he remembered, God's promise kept

games.q: the two laughs — tap the pairs.

s: Sarah never laughed at the promise
she laughed to herself in disbelief, then denied it.
Isaac's name means he will laugh
Yitzchak, from the Hebrew root for laughter.
Rashi says others were blessed when Sarah was remembered
other childless women, the sick, and laughter in the whole world.

games.q: you're Sarah. you've finally given birth, at about ninety. what do you say?
o: don't tell anyone; they'll laugh at me.
God has made laughter for me; all who hear will laugh with me.
games.why: Sarah turns the laugh outward: everyone who hears will laugh with me. the laugh of doubt becomes a laugh of joy.

practice: Think of a time something you'd given up on actually happened, big or small, and remember the laugh or the smile that came out of you. Let it come back into your face now, even a little.
Then picture the people you'd want to share it with, and let the joy spread out to them: everyone who hears will laugh with me.

wordCard.voice: Vayera. The portion where Sarah's laugh of disbelief becomes a laugh of joy, and her son is named Isaac, he will laugh.

orig.note: Hebrew: Isaac, meaning he will laugh.

carryVoice: Your line: laugh with me. Her laugh had room for everyone. Day one hundred seventy-nine, done.

sources.q: Is any thing too hard for the LORD?
